newsitem.title: USA: Western U.S. pounded by freezing rain, snow.
newsitem.headline: Western U.S. pounded by freezing rain, snow.

text.p: Snow and freezing rain pounded the Western United States on Thursday, ruining the holiday travel plans of thousands and causing power outages and traffic tie-ups from northern California to Washington.

The icy weather knocked out power at Portland International Airport, forcing flight delays and cancellations that stranded travelers for hours. The power was restored later, but flights remained behind schedule.
"We're through the worst of it," Portland airport spokesman Darrel Buttice said. "It (the outage) caused cancellation of flights and delays on certainly one of the busiest days of the year."
As many as 100,000 Oregonians in the Portland area lost power in the storm. But National Weather Service forecaster Ira Kosovitz said the worst appeared over.
"Things have calmed down," Kosovitz said from Portland. "But we're still going to get bouts of freezing rain."

Several inches of fresh snow fell in the Seattle area, causing traffic accidents and other problems for holiday shoppers and travelers. Washington state officials warned that the storm would increase the likelihood of flooding.
"There has been a lot of rain and snow, a lot of accidents this morning on the highways," said Linda Ramsey, director of Washington state's emergency management division.
Puget Sound Power and Light Co., which services nine counties in western Washington state, said about 17,600 of its customers were without power late on Thursday.

While Washington and Oregon took a beating, northern and central California saw moderate rain as well as snow at higher elevations. Lengthy flight delays were reported at San Francisco International Airport. Major mountain highways in California and Nevada remained open despite several weather-related accidents.

But the National Weather Service issued a warning on Thursday that a second storm could hit California this weekend. The powerful Pacific storm was expected to reach the state's northern coast late on Friday or Saturday, bringing with it strong gusty winds, heavy rains and more snow.
The approaching storm, just north of the Hawaiian islands, could dump more than 10 inches (25 cm) of rain in some areas and cause flash flooding, forecasters said.
This weekend's storm "is looking to be a big one," National Weather Service forecaster Bob Diaz said. "There is the potential for flooding."
The storm could also wreak havoc on the Sierra Nevada, where residents are still digging out from the last pounding.

Last weekend, more than nine feet (3 metres) of snow fell in some parts of the popular Lake Tahoe ski resort area on the northern California-Nevada border. That blustery storm affected about 100,000 Pacific Gas & Electric Co. customers in the Sierras. Power has been restored to nearly everyone.
PG&E said it was preparing for the incoming storm.
"We're always keeping one eye on the weather and taking the steps that have to be taken in advance," PG&E spokesman Leonard Anderson said.
